subject: Agricultural Science
practicalPaper: Paper 3 is a 1½-hour practical paper of four compulsory questions for 60 marks (an alternative-to-practical paper for private candidates). Candidates identify and draw specimens (soils, rocks, crops, weeds, pests, tools, feeds, parasites), interpret experiments and data on soil properties, seed quality and animal production, and carry out related calculations such as percentages, seed rates and ration formulation.

practicals.title: Soil texture by feel and sieving; fertile versus infertile soil
practicals.topic: Practical: Soil
practicals.aim: To identify soil samples as sandy, loamy or clayey by feeling them wet and dry, to estimate the proportion of particle sizes by sieving, and to compare a fertile with an infertile soil.
apparatus: Set of soil sieves (2 mm, 0.2 mm, 0.05 mm) with pan
materials: Air-dried samples of sandy, loamy and clay soil from the school farm (labelled X, Y, Z)
A dark, crumbly topsoil from under a fallow or compost heap
A pale, hard subsoil or eroded soil from a footpath
safety: Wash hands after handling soil; cover cuts, as soil may carry tetanus spores.
Do not taste soil or rub eyes with soiled hands.
Pick out sharp stones, glass and nails before handling.
procedure: Rub a pinch of each dry soil between thumb and fingers and note whether it feels gritty, smooth (floury) or hard and lumpy.
Moisten a teaspoon of each soil with a few drops of water and knead it into a ball; note whether it falls apart, holds together, or becomes sticky and plastic.
Try to roll each moist ball into a thread about 3 mm thick and bend it into a ring; record whether it breaks at once, cracks, or forms an unbroken ring.
Weigh 50.0 g of the air-dried loamy soil, crush clods gently and pass it through the stack of sieves by shaking for five minutes.
Weigh the fraction retained on each sieve and in the pan, and calculate each as a percentage of the 50.0 g.
Spread the fertile and infertile samples side by side on white tiles; compare colour, crumb structure, plant remains and living organisms (earthworms, termites, roots) using a hand lens.
Record all observations in a table and draw conclusions.
practicals.expectedObservations: Sandy soil feels gritty, will not form a ball and falls apart. Loamy soil feels smooth to slightly gritty and forms a ball that cracks when rolled into a thread. Clay soil is hard and lumpy when dry, sticky and plastic when wet, and rolls into an unbroken ring. The fertile soil is dark brown to black, crumbly, smells earthy and contains humus, roots and earthworms; the infertile soil is pale, compact or loose, and has few or no living organisms.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 50.0 g of loamy soil gave coarse sand 12.5 g, fine sand 18.0 g, silt 9.0 g and clay (pan) 10.5 g. Percentage = mass of fraction ÷ 50.0 × 100: coarse sand 25 %, fine sand 36 %, silt 18 %, clay 21 %. Total sand = 25 + 36 = 61 %. A soil with about 61 % sand, 18 % silt and 21 % clay is a sandy clay loam. Check: 25 + 36 + 18 + 21 = 100 %.
precautions: Use air-dried soil and crush clods gently without grinding the particles.
Shake the sieves for the same length of time for every sample.
Brush every sieve clean before the next sample to avoid carry-over.
Add water to the feel test drop by drop so the soil is moist, not runny.
sourcesOfError: Clay aggregates not broken up, so they are counted as sand.
Loss of fine particles as dust during sieving.
The feel test is subjective and depends on the amount of water added.
commonMistakes: Calling a dark soil 'clay' because of its colour; colour indicates humus, not texture.
Forgetting that the percentages must add up to 100.
Describing sandy soil as 'sticky'.
examTips: WAEC often gives three labelled samples: name each and give one feel feature as the reason.
State fertility indicators in pairs: dark colour (humus), crumb structure, presence of earthworms.
Show the formula (mass of fraction ÷ total mass × 100) before substituting.

practicals.title: Describing and drawing a soil profile
practicals.topic: Practical: Soil profile
practicals.aim: To dig a soil pit, identify the horizons of the soil profile and draw the profile to scale.
materials: A level site on the school farm away from paths and buildings
Water for testing texture
safety: Work in pairs; cut steps into one side of the pit so nobody is trapped.
Keep tools away from the edge so they do not fall on anyone.
Fill the pit or fence it off after the lesson so no person or animal falls in.
procedure: Peg out a pit about 1 m wide and 1.5 m long and dig it to about 1.5 m or to bedrock, leaving one face smooth and vertical (the study face) and the opposite side stepped.
Clean the study face with a cutlass from top to bottom so fresh soil is exposed.
Note changes in colour, texture, structure, root density and stones down the face, and push pegs in where each horizon changes.
Measure the depth of the top and bottom of each horizon from the ground surface with the tape.
Collect a small sample from each horizon in labelled bags for texture and colour tests.
Draw the profile to scale (e.g. 1 cm on paper = 10 cm of soil), shading each horizon and labelling it O, A, B, C and R.
Write a short description of each horizon beside the drawing.
practicals.expectedObservations: O horizon: thin layer of leaves and decaying litter. A horizon (topsoil): dark, crumbly, rich in humus, roots and soil organisms. B horizon (subsoil): lighter brown, red or yellow, more compact, often with accumulated clay and iron and few roots. C horizon: partly weathered parent material with rock fragments. R: solid bedrock (not always reached).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: in a 150 cm pit the horizons measured O 0–5 cm, A 5–30 cm, B 30–90 cm and C 90–150 cm. Thicknesses: O = 5 cm, A = 25 cm, B = 60 cm, C = 60 cm (total 150 cm). At a scale of 1 cm : 10 cm the drawing is 15.0 cm tall, with A drawn 2.5 cm and B drawn 6.0 cm. The A horizon makes up 25 ÷ 150 × 100 = 16.7 % of the profile depth.
precautions: Choose an undisturbed site (not a refuse dump or recently filled ground).
Study a freshly cleaned face in good daylight.
Measure all depths from the same ground-surface reference.
sourcesOfError: Horizon boundaries are often gradual, so depths are estimates.
Soil smeared by the spade hides true colour and structure.
Moist and dry soil differ in colour.
commonMistakes: Drawing horizons of equal thickness instead of to scale.
Omitting the scale and title on the drawing.
Labelling the subsoil as 'topsoil'.
examTips: Drawings need a title, a stated scale, clean continuous lines and labels with ruled guidelines.
Give one distinguishing feature per horizon, e.g. 'A: dark due to humus'.
Know that most plant roots and soil organisms are in the A horizon.

checkQuestions.explanation: Decomposed organic matter accumulates in the topsoil (A).

checkQuestions.explanation: Materials washed down from A are deposited in the subsoil (B).

checkQuestions.explanation: The C horizon is weathering parent material above bedrock.

practicals.title: Identifying igneous, sedimentary and metamorphic rocks
practicals.topic: Practical: Rocks
practicals.aim: To identify common rock specimens by their visible features and simple tests, and relate them to the soils they form.
apparatus: Dropping bottle of dilute hydrochloric acid
materials: Rock specimens: granite, basalt, sandstone, shale, limestone, marble, quartzite, gneiss (collected locally or from a rock kit)
Water
safety: Wear goggles when using acid and wipe spills at once.
Handle the knife carefully when scratching rocks.
Do not strike rocks with hammers near other students.
procedure: Examine each specimen with a hand lens and record colour, grain size, whether grains are crystals or rounded particles, layering (bedding or banding) and any fossils.
Scratch each rock with a steel nail; record whether it scratches easily (soft) or not (hard).
Add a drop of dilute acid to each rock and look for effervescence.
Weigh one rock, then find its volume by lowering it on a thread into a measuring cylinder of water and reading the rise in water level.
Calculate its density.
Classify each rock as igneous, sedimentary or metamorphic and record the evidence.
practicals.expectedObservations: Granite: hard, speckled with interlocking crystals (pink/white feldspar, glassy quartz, black mica), no layers – igneous. Basalt: dark, fine-grained, heavy – igneous. Sandstone: rounded sand grains cemented together, gritty, may show layers – sedimentary. Shale: fine, soft, splits into thin layers – sedimentary. Limestone: fizzes with acid, may contain fossils – sedimentary. Marble: crystalline, fizzes with acid – metamorphic. Gneiss: alternating light and dark bands – metamorphic. Quartzite: very hard, sugary texture, does not fizz – metamorphic.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a rock weighed 81.0 g. Water in the cylinder rose from 50.0 cm³ to 80.0 cm³, so its volume = 80.0 − 50.0 = 30.0 cm³. Density = mass ÷ volume = 81.0 ÷ 30.0 = 2.70 g/cm³, typical of granite, limestone or marble; a fizz with acid would point to limestone or marble.
precautions: Use clean, freshly broken surfaces for observation.
Read the measuring cylinder at eye level at the bottom of the meniscus.
Make sure the rock is fully submerged with no air bubbles clinging to it.
sourcesOfError: Weathered surfaces hide true colour and texture.
Porous rocks absorb water, lowering the volume reading.
Parallax when reading the cylinder.
commonMistakes: Confusing bedding in sedimentary rock with banding in gneiss.
Saying granite fizzes with acid.
Giving density without units.
examTips: Give the rock type AND one observable reason, e.g. 'igneous – interlocking crystals, no layers'.
Link rocks to soils: granite weathers to sandy or loamy soils, shale to clay soils, limestone to alkaline soils.
Remember metamorphic means changed by heat and pressure: marble from limestone, slate from shale.

checkQuestions.explanation: Marble and limestone contain calcium carbonate, which reacts with acid releasing carbon dioxide.

checkQuestions.q: Interlocking crystals and no layers suggest a rock that is
checkQuestions.explanation: Igneous rocks form by cooling of magma into crystals.

practicals.title: Mechanical analysis of soil by sedimentation
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To separate a soil sample into gravel, sand, silt and clay by sedimentation and estimate their proportions.
apparatus: 250 cm³ measuring cylinder or tall transparent bottle with stopper
materials: About 50 cm³ of air-dried soil
Water
A pinch of washing soda (dispersing agent, optional)
safety: Hold the cylinder firmly when shaking; glass breaks easily.
Wipe up spilled water to avoid slipping.
procedure: Put soil into the cylinder to about one-quarter of its height.
Add water until the cylinder is about three-quarters full and add a pinch of dispersing agent.
Stopper and shake vigorously for two minutes to break up aggregates.
Stand the cylinder on a level bench and leave it undisturbed for at least 24 hours.
Observe the layers that settle and measure the thickness of each with a ruler.
Calculate each layer as a percentage of the total settled height and draw a labelled diagram of the cylinder.
practicals.expectedObservations: Gravel and coarse sand settle first at the bottom, then fine sand, then silt; clay settles last as the top layer and some stays suspended, so the water remains cloudy. Organic matter (humus) floats on the surface.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: after 24 hours the layers measured gravel 4 mm, sand 20 mm, silt 10 mm and clay 6 mm. Total = 4 + 20 + 10 + 6 = 40 mm. Gravel = 4 ÷ 40 × 100 = 10 %; sand = 20 ÷ 40 × 100 = 50 %; silt = 25 %; clay = 15 %. The soil is mainly sand with moderate silt and some clay, so it is a sandy loam.
precautions: Shake thoroughly so all aggregates are dispersed.
Do not disturb the cylinder while particles are settling.
Measure each layer at eye level against the ruler.
sourcesOfError: Boundaries between layers are not sharp.
Some clay remains suspended and is not measured.
Settled particles are loosely packed, so heights only approximate mass proportions.
commonMistakes: Drawing clay at the bottom of the cylinder.
Forgetting to label the floating organic matter.
Calculating percentages from the height of water instead of the settled soil.
examTips: Explain the order of settling: larger, heavier particles settle faster.
Your diagram must show the layers in the correct order with labels and a title.
State why the water stays cloudy: fine clay particles remain in suspension as colloids.

checkQuestions.explanation: Heavier, larger particles sink fastest.

checkQuestions.q: The material that floats on the water surface is
checkQuestions.explanation: Humus is less dense than water.

checkQuestions.explanation: Colloidal clay settles very slowly.

practicals.title: Bulk density and total pore space of soil
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To determine the bulk density of an undisturbed soil core and calculate its total pore space.
apparatus: Metal core sampler (cylinder) of known dimensions
materials: Field soil on the school farm
Moisture can or foil tray
safety: Use oven gloves when removing samples from the oven.
Keep fingers clear when driving the core in with the mallet.
procedure: Measure the internal radius and height of the core sampler and calculate its volume (V = πr²h).
Drive the sampler vertically into the soil with the mallet over a wooden block until its top is level with the soil surface.
Dig the core out carefully, trim both ends flush with a knife and transfer all the soil to a weighed can.
Dry at 105 °C to constant mass (about 24 hours), cool in a desiccator and weigh.
Calculate bulk density = oven-dry mass ÷ core volume.
Calculate total pore space = (1 − bulk density ÷ particle density) × 100, taking particle density as 2.65 g/cm³.
practicals.expectedObservations: Sandy soils give higher bulk density (about 1.5–1.7 g/cm³) than loams and clays (about 1.1–1.4 g/cm³). Compacted soil from a footpath gives a higher bulk density and lower pore space than soil from a cultivated bed.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: core radius 2.5 cm, height 10.0 cm. Volume = 3.142 × 2.5² × 10.0 = 196.4 cm³. Oven-dry soil = 255.3 g. Bulk density = 255.3 ÷ 196.4 = 1.30 g/cm³. Total pore space = (1 − 1.30 ÷ 2.65) × 100 = (1 − 0.491) × 100 = 50.9 %.
precautions: Do not compress the core while driving it in.
Trim the ends exactly level with the cylinder.
Dry to constant mass so all water is removed.
sourcesOfError: Compaction or loss of soil while sampling changes the true volume.
Stones inside the core raise the mass.
Incomplete drying gives a high mass.
commonMistakes: Using moist mass instead of oven-dry mass.
Using diameter instead of radius in πr²h.
Writing pore space without the % sign.
examTips: Always state the formula, substitute with units and give the answer to the required decimal places.
Remember: higher bulk density means more compaction and less pore space.
Particle density of most mineral soils is about 2.65 g/cm³.

If bulk density is 1.59 g/cm³ and particle density 2.65 g/cm³, total pore space is
Compaction of soil by heavy machinery
checkQuestions.explanation: Particles are pressed together, so more mass occupies the same volume.

checkQuestions.q: The soil is dried at 105 °C in order to
checkQuestions.explanation: 105 °C drives off water without burning organic matter.

practicals.title: Determining the moisture content of a moist soil
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To determine the percentage moisture content of a fresh soil sample by oven drying.
apparatus: Moisture can or evaporating dish with lid
materials: Freshly collected moist soil in a sealed polythene bag
safety: Use tongs or gloves to handle hot cans.
Do not open the oven door with your face close to it.
procedure: Weigh a clean, dry, empty can (W1).
Add about 50 g of fresh moist soil, close the lid and weigh again (W2).
Remove the lid and dry the can and soil in an oven at 105 °C for 24 hours.
Cool in a desiccator, replace the lid and weigh (W3).
Re-heat, cool and re-weigh until two weighings agree (constant mass).
Calculate the mass of water and the moisture content on a dry-mass basis and on a wet-mass basis.
practicals.expectedObservations: The soil becomes lighter in colour and loses mass on drying. Clay and humus-rich soils lose more water than sandy soil collected at the same time.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: W1 = 25.00 g, W2 = 75.00 g, W3 = 65.00 g. Mass of water = W2 − W3 = 10.00 g. Mass of dry soil = W3 − W1 = 40.00 g. Moisture content (dry basis) = 10.00 ÷ 40.00 × 100 = 25.0 %. Moisture content (wet basis) = 10.00 ÷ (W2 − W1 = 50.00) × 100 = 20.0 %. State which basis the question asks for.
precautions: Keep the fresh sample sealed until weighing so it does not dry out.
Cool the can in a desiccator so it does not absorb moisture from the air.
Heat to constant mass.
sourcesOfError: Water lost from the sample between field and laboratory.
Weighing while still warm (convection currents lower the reading).
Some organic matter may be lost if overheated.
commonMistakes: Subtracting in the wrong order (W3 − W2).
Using the mass of soil plus can as the soil mass.
Mixing up dry-basis and wet-basis percentages.
examTips: Set out the subtraction steps clearly; method marks are given for each step.
Moisture is usually expressed as a percentage of the dry soil unless the question says otherwise – read carefully.
A common follow-up asks why the soil is cooled in a desiccator: to prevent re-absorption of moisture.

checkQuestions.q: Why is a desiccator used?
options: To keep the dried soil from absorbing moisture as it cools
checkQuestions.explanation: The desiccant keeps the air around the sample dry.

practicals.title: Water-holding capacity and drainage of sand, loam and clay
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To compare the volume of water retained and the rate of drainage of sandy, loamy and clay soils.
materials: 100 g each of oven-dried sandy, loamy and clay soil
Water
safety: Clamp funnels firmly so the stands do not topple.
Mop up spilled water.
procedure: Plug the neck of each funnel loosely with the same amount of cotton wool and place each over a measuring cylinder.
Put 100 g of each dry soil into a funnel and label them A (sand), B (loam) and C (clay).
Pour 100 cm³ of water gently and at the same time onto each soil.
Start the stopwatch and record the time the first drop falls and the volume collected after 5, 10, 30 and 60 minutes.
After 60 minutes record the final volume in each cylinder.
Calculate the water retained and the water-holding capacity as a percentage of the dry soil mass.
practicals.expectedObservations: Water drains quickest through sand and the largest volume is collected below it. Clay drains slowly, the least water is collected and water may stand on its surface. Loam is intermediate.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: after 1 hour the volumes collected were sand 70 cm³, loam 58 cm³, clay 40 cm³. Water retained = 100 − volume collected: sand 30 cm³, loam 42 cm³, clay 60 cm³. Taking 1 cm³ of water = 1 g, water-holding capacity = retained ÷ 100 g × 100: sand 30 %, loam 42 %, clay 60 %. Average drainage rate through sand = 70 cm³ ÷ 60 min = 1.17 cm³/min.
precautions: Use equal masses of soil and equal volumes of water for all funnels.
Use the same amount of cotton wool in each funnel.
Pour water gently so soil is not washed through.
sourcesOfError: Some water evaporates or wets the cotton wool and funnel.
Soils packed to different degrees.
Water not added to all funnels at exactly the same time.
commonMistakes: Reporting the volume collected as the volume retained.
Concluding that sand is best for crops because it drains well, ignoring drought risk.
Not using oven-dried soil.
examTips: Expect a labelled set-up diagram: funnel, cotton wool, soil, cylinder and stand.
Link results to farming: clay waterlogs, sand dries out, loam is ideal.
Give at least two precautions, worded as actions.

checkQuestions.q: 100 cm³ of water is poured on 100 g of clay and 35 cm³ is collected. The water-holding capacity is
Which soil drains fastest?
checkQuestions.explanation: Sand has large pore spaces between its grains.

checkQuestions.q: The cotton wool in the funnel
checkQuestions.explanation: It holds the soil while allowing water through.

checkQuestions.q: Which soil is most likely to become waterlogged?
checkQuestions.explanation: Fine pores in clay slow drainage.

practicals.title: Capillary rise of water in different soils
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on physical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To compare the rate and height of capillary rise of water in sandy, loamy and clay soils.
apparatus: Three glass or clear plastic tubes about 30–50 cm long
Cotton wool or muslin and rubber bands
materials: Dry, finely crushed sandy, loamy and clay soil
Water
safety: Handle glass tubes carefully; check for chipped ends.
Keep the trough stable on the bench.
procedure: Tie cotton wool or muslin over the lower end of each tube.
Fill each tube with one dry soil, tapping gently and equally to pack it.
Clamp the tubes upright with their lower ends dipping to the same depth (about 2 cm) in water in the trough.
Start the stopwatch and measure the height of the wetted soil above the water surface after 10, 20, 30 and 60 minutes, and again after 24 hours.
Record the results in a table and plot height against time for each soil on the same axes.
Calculate the rate of rise for the stated time intervals.
practicals.expectedObservations: Water rises fastest at first in sand because its wide pores offer little resistance, but it stops at a low height. Water rises slowly in clay but eventually reaches the greatest height because its pores are very fine. Loam is intermediate.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: in sand the water rose 3.0 cm in the first 10 minutes, so the initial rate = 3.0 ÷ 10 = 0.30 cm/min. In loam the height was 8.4 cm after 60 minutes, so the average rate = 8.4 ÷ 60 = 0.14 cm/min. After 24 hours clay had reached 21.0 cm compared with sand 7.0 cm: clay rose 21.0 ÷ 7.0 = 3 times as high.
precautions: Pack all tubes to the same degree.
Dip all tubes to the same depth and start timing together.
Measure from the water surface, not from the bottom of the tube.
sourcesOfError: Unequal packing.
The wetting front is irregular, making readings approximate.
The water level in the trough falls as water is taken up.
commonMistakes: Concluding that sand has the highest capillarity because it rose fastest at first.
Plotting time on the vertical axis.
Joining graph points with ruled straight lines instead of a smooth curve.
examTips: Distinguish rate (speed) of rise from final height – a favourite WAEC trap.
On graphs: title, labelled axes with units, sensible scale and a key for the three soils.
Relate capillarity to the water supply to plant roots during dry periods.

checkQuestions.q: Water rises 4.5 cm in 15 minutes. The rate of capillary rise is
Over 24 hours the greatest capillary height is usually reached in
checkQuestions.explanation: Fine pores give the greatest capillary pull.

checkQuestions.q: Capillary rise is important to crops because it
options: supplies water from lower layers to roots
checkQuestions.explanation: Water moves up towards the root zone as surface soil dries.

checkQuestions.q: Which is a precaution in this experiment?
options: Dip the tubes to different depths
Pack the soils to the same degree
checkQuestions.explanation: Equal packing makes the comparison fair.

practicals.title: Determining soil pH and liming needs
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on chemical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To determine the pH of soil samples using universal indicator (or a pH meter) and decide whether liming is needed.
apparatus: pH meter (if available) or universal indicator with colour chart
materials: Soil samples from different plots
Distilled water
Barium sulphate powder (optional, to settle clay)
safety: Do not taste or swallow the indicator; wash off skin contact.
Handle the pH electrode gently; it is made of glass.
procedure: Weigh 10 g of air-dried soil into a beaker and add 25 cm³ of distilled water (1 : 2.5 ratio).
Stir well for one minute and allow to stand for 30 minutes, stirring occasionally.
Filter into a clean test tube (add a little barium sulphate first if the filtrate is cloudy).
Add three drops of universal indicator, shake and match the colour against the chart; or dip a calibrated pH meter electrode into the suspension and read.
Repeat for each sample and record the pH.
Use the pH to classify each soil and recommend liming where the pH is below about 5.5 for most crops.
practicals.expectedObservations: Universal indicator gives red/orange (pH 4–5) for strongly acidic soils common in high-rainfall southern Nigeria, yellow-green (pH 6–7) for near-neutral soils, and blue (pH 8 and above) for alkaline soils found in some northern areas or over limestone.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: Plot A had pH 5.0 and Plot B pH 6.0. Since pH is logarithmic, the hydrogen ion concentration in A is 10^(6.0 − 5.0) = 10 times that in B. The extension officer recommends 2.0 t/ha of agricultural lime for Plot A. Plot A measures 50 m × 50 m = 2 500 m² = 0.25 ha, so lime needed = 2.0 × 0.25 = 0.5 t = 500 kg.
precautions: Use distilled water, not tap water, which may alter the pH.
Rinse the electrode or test tube between samples.
Calibrate the pH meter with buffer solutions before use.
sourcesOfError: Colour matching is subjective.
A muddy filtrate masks the indicator colour.
The sample may not represent the whole plot.
commonMistakes: Saying a soil of pH 8 is acidic.
Assuming a pH difference of 1 means twice as acidic.
Recommending lime for an alkaline soil.
examTips: State the colour observed AND the inference (e.g. 'orange – acidic, pH about 5').
Give the correction: acidic soil – liming; alkaline soil – sulphur or acid-forming fertilisers such as ammonium sulphate.
Show the unit conversion: 10 000 m² = 1 ha.

checkQuestions.explanation: One pH unit is a factor of 10.

practicals.title: Organic matter content of soil by loss on ignition
practicals.topic: Practical: Laboratory work on chemical properties of soil
practicals.aim: To determine the percentage of organic matter in a soil sample by heating it strongly.
apparatus: Bunsen burner, tripod and pipe-clay triangle
materials: Oven-dried topsoil sample (sieved through 2 mm)
safety: Wear goggles; hot crucibles can crack.
Use tongs and place hot crucibles on a heat-proof mat.
Keep hair and clothing away from the flame.
procedure: Weigh a clean, dry crucible (W1).
Add about 20 g of oven-dried soil and weigh again (W2).
Heat strongly over a Bunsen burner for 20–30 minutes, stirring occasionally, until no more smoke is seen and the soil turns reddish or grey.
Cool in a desiccator and weigh (W3).
Re-heat, cool and re-weigh until constant mass.
Calculate the loss in mass and the percentage of organic matter.
practicals.expectedObservations: Smoke and a burning smell are given off as organic matter burns; the soil becomes lighter in colour (often reddish-brown) and loses mass.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: W1 = 18.40 g, W2 = 38.40 g, W3 = 37.20 g. Mass of dry soil = 38.40 − 18.40 = 20.00 g. Loss in mass = 38.40 − 37.20 = 1.20 g. Organic matter = 1.20 ÷ 20.00 × 100 = 6.0 %.
precautions: Use oven-dried soil so the loss in mass is due to organic matter, not water.
Heat to constant mass.
Cool in a desiccator before weighing.
sourcesOfError: Some soil may spit out of the crucible.
Loss of water held within clay minerals overestimates organic matter.
Incomplete burning underestimates it.
commonMistakes: Using fresh moist soil.
Dividing the loss by W2 instead of by the soil mass.
Weighing the crucible while hot.

Samples of poultry droppings, cow dung (farmyard manure), compost and green manure (e.g. Mucuna leaves)
Water
safety: Wear gloves; some fertilisers irritate skin and eyes.
Wash hands after handling manures, which carry pathogens.
Never taste fertilisers.
procedure: Examine each fertiliser for colour, granule shape and size, smell and whether it absorbs moisture from the air.
Dissolve a little of each in water in a test tube and note its solubility.
Read the bag label for the nutrient grade (N-P₂O₅-K₂O) and record it.
Examine each manure for colour, odour, texture and visible plant remains.
Measure the length and breadth of a demonstration plot.
Calculate the mass of fertiliser and manure needed for the plot at the recommended rates.
State the method of application (broadcasting, side placement, ring placement, foliar spray, or working manure into the soil during land preparation).
practicals.expectedObservations: Urea: white, round prills, very soluble, absorbs moisture. Muriate of potash: pink-red crystals. Single superphosphate: grey granules, partly soluble. NPK: mixed-coloured granules. Poultry droppings: grey-white with a strong ammonia smell. Compost: dark, crumbly, earthy smell with little odour.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example 1: a maize plot of 20 m × 15 m = 300 m² = 0.03 ha needs 60 kg N/ha from NPK 15-15-15. Fertiliser per hectare = 60 ÷ 0.15 = 400 kg/ha; for the plot = 400 × 0.03 = 12 kg. Worked example 2: urea contains 46 % N, so to supply 46 kg N/ha you need 46 ÷ 0.46 = 100 kg urea/ha. Forgetting to convert m² to hectares.
Confusing muriate of potash (KCl) with a nitrogen fertiliser.

For manures, give one advantage (improves structure) and one disadvantage (bulky, slow release).

Water source (tap or well)
safety: Keep electric pumps away from water spills; switch off before handling.
Do not drink untreated well or drainage water.
Wear boots when digging drainage channels.
procedure: Identify each piece of equipment and state one use and one maintenance practice.
Measure the length and width of a seedbed and calculate its area.
Decide the depth of water to apply (e.g. 10 mm) and calculate the volume needed.
Find the volume of the watering can by filling it from a measuring container.
Calculate the number of cans needed, then water the bed evenly with the rose held low.
Dig a short open drain (about 30 cm deep) along the lower side of a waterlogged area and observe the water flow.
Clean and store the equipment after use.
practicals.expectedObservations: A rose breaks the water into fine drops that do not wash out seeds. Sprinklers wet a circular area. Drip lines wet only the root zone and save water. Water collects in the drain and flows away, leaving the surrounding soil less soggy.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: bed 5 m × 1 m = 5 m². 10 mm of water = 0.010 m depth, so volume = 5 × 0.010 = 0.05 m³ = 50 litres (1 mm over 1 m² = 1 litre). With a 10-litre can, 50 ÷ 10 = 5 cans are needed per watering. Watering twice daily for 7 days uses 50 × 2 × 7 = 700 litres.

Hold the rose close to the soil so seedlings are not damaged.

The can not filled to the same level every time.
Evaporation and run-off reduce the water reaching the soil.

Forgetting that 1 mm of water on 1 m² equals 1 litre.
Using a can without a rose on young seedlings.

Name the types of irrigation: surface (furrow, basin, flood), sprinkler, drip and sub-surface.
Name the types of drainage: surface (open ditches) and sub-surface (tile or pipe drains).

practicals.title: Identification, use and maintenance of simple farm tools
practicals.topic: Practical: Farm tools and equipment
practicals.aim: To identify common farm tools, state their uses, draw them and carry out routine maintenance.
apparatus: Hoe, long-handled hoe, cutlass, garden trowel, hand fork, shovel, spade, rake, sickle, secateurs, shears, pruner, budding knife, emasculator, wheelbarrow, watering can
Wire brush, rags, used engine oil or grease
materials: A small overgrown plot on the school farm
safety: Carry cutlasses and sickles with the blade pointing down and away from the body.
Keep a safe distance (at least 2 m) between students working with cutting tools.
Wear boots and gloves; never leave tools lying in grass.
procedure: Lay the tools out on a bench, identify each and state its main use (e.g. cutlass – clearing bush; hand fork – loosening soil around seedlings).
Draw and label one tool (e.g. a hoe: blade, handle, socket/tang) with a title and magnification or scale.
Use the cutlass and hoe to clear and till a measured strip of the plot, noting the time taken.
After use, wash off soil, dry the tools and scrape off rust with a wire brush.
Sharpen the cutlass and hoe with a file at the correct angle, filing away from the body.
Oil or grease metal parts, tighten loose handles and store the tools in a dry, roofed store, hanging long-handled tools.
practicals.expectedObservations: Sharp, clean tools cut and till faster and with less effort. Tools left unwashed rust and handles crack if left in the sun and rain.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a student cleared a 10 m × 5 m strip (50 m²) in 1 hour. At this rate one worker clears 50 × 8 = 400 m² in an 8-hour day, so the class figure is taken as about 0.05 ha (500 m²) per man-day for a fitter adult. To clear 0.25 ha: 0.25 ÷ 0.05 = 5 man-days. Two workers need 5 ÷ 2 = 2.5 days. At ₦3 000 per man-day the labour cost is 5 × ₦3 000 = ₦15 000.
precautions: Use each tool only for its intended purpose.
File the blade away from the body.
Store tools clean, dry and oiled.
sourcesOfError: Work rate depends on vegetation density and the worker's fitness.
Time recorded loosely.
commonMistakes: Confusing a spade (flat blade, for digging) with a shovel (scooped blade, for moving loose material).
Giving 'cleaning' as the only maintenance practice for every tool.
Drawing tools without labels or title.
examTips: Typical question: identify specimens A–D, state one use and one maintenance practice each.
Maintenance answers that score: wash after use, oil metal parts, sharpen blades, replace broken handles, store in a dry place.
In drawings, show proportions correctly and label at least three parts.

checkQuestions.explanation: The cutlass is the main clearing tool.

practicals.title: Tractor- and animal-drawn implements and field capacity
practicals.topic: Practical: Tractor and animal drawn implements
practicals.aim: To identify ploughs, harrows, ridgers, planters and cultivators, name their main parts and calculate the field capacity of an implement.
apparatus: Disc plough, mouldboard plough, disc harrow, spike-tooth harrow, ridger, planter, cultivator (actual implements at a farm centre, or clear pictures)
materials: Grease and engine oil
Rags
safety: Never stand between a tractor and an implement during hitching.
Lower implements to the ground before inspecting them.
Keep clear of sharp discs and tines.
procedure: Identify each implement and state its use and whether it is used for primary or secondary tillage, planting or weeding.
Name the main parts: e.g. disc plough – frame, discs, scrapers, hitch points, depth wheel; mouldboard plough – share, mouldboard, landside, frog.
Measure the working width of the plough or harrow.
Draw and label one implement.
Grease the bearings and nipples, check bolts and clean off soil; coat discs with used oil if they are to be stored.
Calculate the field capacity using the formula below.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ploughs cut and invert the soil (primary tillage); harrows break clods into fine tilth (secondary tillage); ridgers throw soil into ridges; planters meter and place seed; cultivators loosen soil and remove weeds between rows. Animal-drawn implements are lighter and narrower than tractor-drawn ones.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a disc plough with a working width of 1.2 m moves at 5 km/h with a field efficiency of 75 %. Theoretical field capacity = width (m) × speed (km/h) ÷ 10 = 1.2 × 5 ÷ 10 = 0.60 ha/h. Effective field capacity = 0.60 × 0.75 = 0.45 ha/h. Time to plough a 3.6 ha field = 3.6 ÷ 0.45 = 8 hours.
precautions: Inspect implements only when they are lowered and the tractor engine is off.
Use the correct spanner size to avoid rounding bolt heads.
Store implements under a roof, raised off the ground.
sourcesOfError: Field efficiency varies with turning, overlaps and stoppages.
Speed is not constant in the field.
commonMistakes: Calling a harrow a plough because both have discs.
Forgetting to divide by 10 in the field-capacity formula.
Mixing up primary and secondary tillage.
examTips: State one difference between a disc plough and a disc harrow (plough discs larger and fewer, set at an angle to cut and turn the soil; harrow discs smaller, in gangs).
Maintenance answers: grease bearings, tighten bolts, replace worn shares or discs, clean after use, store under shed.
Show the formula, the substitution and the unit (ha/h).

checkQuestions.explanation: The share makes the horizontal cut.

checkQuestions.explanation: The ridger throws soil to both sides to form ridges.

practicals.title: Major components and routine servicing of the farm tractor
practicals.topic: Practical: Farm tractor
practicals.aim: To identify the major parts of a farm tractor and carry out daily and periodic servicing checks.
apparatus: A farm tractor (at the school or a nearby farm centre/ADP station)
Dipstick, tyre pressure gauge, grease gun
materials: Engine oil of the grade in the manual
Diesel
Distilled water for the battery
Grease, clean rags
safety: Only carry out checks with the engine off, key removed and handbrake on.
Allow the engine to cool before opening the radiator cap.
No smoking or naked flames near fuel; wipe spills immediately.
procedure: Walk round the tractor and identify the engine, radiator, air cleaner, fuel tank, battery, clutch, gear box, power take-off (PTO), three-point linkage, hydraulic lift, drawbar, steering, brakes and tyres.
Check the engine oil level with the dipstick and top up to the mark if low.
Check the radiator coolant level (engine cold) and the battery electrolyte level.
Clean or check the air cleaner and check the fan belt tension.
Check tyre pressures with a gauge and inspect for cuts.
Grease all grease nipples on the front axle, steering and linkage.
Record the hour-meter reading in the service log and work out when the next periodic service (e.g. oil change) is due.
practicals.expectedObservations: All fluid levels between the minimum and maximum marks; correct tyre pressures; fresh grease seen emerging at each joint after greasing.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: the manual says change the engine oil every 250 hours. The last change was at 1 000 h and the hour meter now reads 1 180 h, so the next change is due at 1 250 h, i.e. in 1 250 − 1 180 = 70 hours. If the tractor uses 6 litres of diesel per hour and works 8 hours, fuel used = 6 × 8 = 48 litres; at ₦1 000 per litre this costs ₦48 000.
precautions: Check oil with the tractor on level ground.
Use only the fuel and oil grades recommended by the manufacturer.
Keep a written service record.
sourcesOfError: Oil reading taken on a slope or immediately after running.
Inaccurate hour meter.
commonMistakes: Opening a hot radiator.
Confusing the PTO (drives implements) with the drawbar (pulls implements).
Listing 'washing the tractor' as the only maintenance practice.
examTips: Name a part and give its function, e.g. 'PTO – transmits power to rotating implements such as a slasher'.
Separate daily checks (oil, water, fuel, tyres) from periodic servicing (oil and filter change, greasing).
Hour-meter arithmetic questions reward clear steps.

checkQuestions.explanation: The PTO shaft drives rotating implements.

checkQuestions.q: Oil is changed every 200 h. Last change at 600 h; meter now 730 h. Hours to next change:
checkQuestions.explanation: Next due at 800 h; 800 − 730 = 70 h.

checkQuestions.q: Before removing the radiator cap you should
checkQuestions.explanation: Hot coolant under pressure can scald.

checkQuestions.q: Ploughs and harrows are attached to the tractor through the
checkQuestions.explanation: The hydraulic three-point linkage carries mounted implements.

practicals.title: Harvesting, processing and storage equipment
practicals.topic: Practical: Harvesting, processing and storage equipment
practicals.aim: To identify harvesting, processing and storage equipment, state their uses, and measure shelling percentage and drying loss for maize.
materials: Dry maize cobs from the school farm
Tarpaulin
safety: Keep fingers away from the moving parts of shellers and graters.
Wear a dust mask when shelling and winnowing.
Never use pesticide containers to store grain.
procedure: Identify each item and state its use and the crop it is used for.
Weigh a batch of dehusked maize cobs.
Shell the cobs with the sheller, winnow the grain to remove chaff and weigh the clean grain.
Calculate the shelling percentage.
Measure the grain moisture with a meter (or note the value given), spread the grain thinly on a tarpaulin or in a dryer, and dry to safe storage moisture (about 13 %).
Calculate the expected mass after drying and compare with the actual mass.
Store the dry grain in hermetic or clean jute bags on pallets in a ventilated store.
practicals.expectedObservations: The sheller separates grain from the cob; the winnower blows off light chaff. Dried grain rattles and is hard when bitten; the batch loses mass as water evaporates.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example 1: 50 kg of cobs gave 38 kg of grain. Shelling percentage = 38 ÷ 50 × 100 = 76 %. Worked example 2: 100 kg of grain at 20 % moisture is dried to 13 %. Dry matter = 100 × (100 − 20) ÷ 100 = 80 kg, which stays the same. Final mass = 80 ÷ (100 − 13) × 100 = 91.95 kg. Water removed = 100 − 91.95 = 8.05 kg.
precautions: Dry grain on a clean tarpaulin, not bare ground, to avoid contamination and aflatoxin moulds.
Weigh on the same scale before and after.
Store grain only when it is properly dry.
sourcesOfError: Grain lost during shelling and winnowing.
Moisture meter not calibrated.
Uneven drying.
commonMistakes: Calculating moisture loss as 20 − 13 = 7 % of the original mass (7 kg) instead of using the dry-matter method.
Confusing a dehusker with a sheller.
Storing grain in old fertiliser or chemical sacks.
examTips: Identification questions: name, use, and the crop handled (e.g. groundnut lifter – lifting groundnut pods from the soil).
Explain why grain is dried before storage: prevents moulds, germination and insect build-up.
Show the dry-matter step in drying calculations.

checkQuestions.explanation: Winnowing uses air to blow away light chaff.

checkQuestions.explanation: Low moisture stops fungi and slows insects.

practicals.title: Using and maintaining horticultural tools
practicals.topic: Practical: Uses and maintenance of horticultural tools and implements
practicals.aim: To identify and correctly use horticultural tools for planting, pruning and trimming, and to maintain them.
apparatus: Hedge shears, secateurs, pruning knife, budding knife, dibber, hand trowel, hand fork, measuring tape, garden line and pegs, hoe, garden fork
materials: Ornamental hedge (e.g. Ixora, Duranta, Acalypha) in the school compound
Seedlings for planting
safety: Close secateurs and shears with the safety catch when not in use.
Cut away from the body and keep the other hand behind the blade.
Pass sharp tools handle-first.
procedure: Identify each tool and state its use.
Stretch a garden line along a planned hedge row, measure it and mark planting points with pegs at the recommended spacing.
Use the dibber or hand trowel to make planting holes and transplant seedlings at each peg.
Trim an overgrown hedge with shears to an even height and shape, and remove thick branches with secateurs, cutting just above a bud at a slant.
Clean sap and soil off the blades, dry them, sharpen on a stone and oil the pivot and blades.
Store tools closed, in a dry place.

Keep a straight line with a garden line.
Sharpen at the original bevel angle.

Uneven trimming when the shears are not held level.

Using shears to cut thick branches (damages the blades).
Cutting far above a bud, leaving a stub that dies back.

Row-count questions: number of plants = length ÷ spacing + 1 when both ends are planted.
Link pruning to shape, flowering and removal of diseased parts.

practicals.title: Livestock and fishing equipment; egg candling
practicals.topic: Practical: Livestock and fishing equipment
practicals.aim: To identify livestock and fishing equipment, state their uses and care, and use an egg candler to determine fertility and hatchability.

Cast net, gill net, hook and line, fish trap, scoop net

safety: Handle hot branding irons and incubators carefully.
Wash hands after handling eggs and poultry equipment.
Keep hooks covered; nets can entangle feet near water.
procedure: Identify each piece of equipment and state its use and how it is cleaned and maintained (e.g. drinkers washed daily and disinfected).
In a darkened room, hold each egg (day 7 of incubation) broad end against the candler light.
Classify eggs as fertile (dark spot with spider-like blood vessels), clear/infertile (no development) or dead germ (blood ring).
Remove clear eggs and record the numbers.
Record the number of chicks hatched at day 21.
Calculate fertility and hatchability percentages and the feeder space needed for the chicks.

Miscounting cracked or abnormal eggs.

Rounding the number of feeders down.
Confusing a burdizzo (castration) with a debeaker.

For each item give name, use and maintenance.

practicals.title: Chain surveying a plot and calculating its area
practicals.topic: Practical: Farm surveying equipment
practicals.aim: To identify simple surveying equipment and use it to measure a rectangular farm plot and calculate its area.
apparatus: Gunter's chain or 30 m measuring tape
materials: An open area of the school farm
safety: Do not throw ranging poles or arrows.
Watch for snakes and holes in long grass; wear boots.
Handle the chain carefully to avoid kinks that injure hands.
procedure: Identify each piece of equipment and state its use.
Place ranging poles at the four corners of the plot so that each side can be seen in a straight line.
Two students chain each side: the leader carries the chain and arrows, the follower holds the zero end at the station; insert an arrow at each full chain length.
Count arrows to find the number of full chains and add the remaining links or metres.
Use the plumb bob when chaining on slopes, and the compass to take the bearing of each side.
Record measurements in the field book and draw the plot to scale.

Line up the ranging poles so you chain in a straight line.
Hold the chain horizontally on slopes and use a plumb bob.

Not following a straight line between stations.
Miscounting arrows.

Dividing m² by 1 000 instead of 10 000 to get hectares.
Recording links as metres.
examTips: Know the uses: ranging poles – mark stations and straight lines; arrows – count chain lengths; offset staff – measure short perpendicular offsets.

Write units at every step of area calculations.

practicals.title: Identifying seeds, seedlings, fruits and storage organs of crops
practicals.topic: Practical: Seeds, seedlings, fruits and storage organs of crops
practicals.aim: To identify seeds, seedlings, fruits and storage organs of common crops, pasture grasses and legumes, and to draw and label them.

safety: Cut away from fingers on a tile.
Do not eat treated seeds; many are dressed with fungicide.
Wash hands after handling seeds and cassava (contains cyanogenic compounds).
procedure: Examine each seed and note its shape, colour, size and whether it is monocotyledonous or dicotyledonous; split soaked seeds to see cotyledons or endosperm.

practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 100 maize grains weighed 30.0 g, so 1 000 grains weigh 300 g and 1 kg contains 1 000 ÷ 0.30 = 3 333 grains (about 3 300). 100 cowpea seeds weighed 20.0 g, so 1 kg contains 1 000 ÷ 0.20 = 5 000 seeds. Draw from the specimen, not from memory.
Weigh a fresh count of seeds that are clean and whole.

Miscounting seeds.

Calling the maize grain a seed without mentioning it is a fruit (caryopsis).
Drawings too small or shaded instead of clean lines.

practicals.title: Field and storage pests of crops and damage assessment
practicals.topic: Practical: Main pests and diseases of crops
practicals.aim: To identify the main field and storage pests of crops, describe their damage and control, and estimate the percentage of damage.

Damaged plant parts and stored grain
safety: Wear gloves when handling grain treated with insecticide.
Do not taste stored produce.
Use forceps for insects that bite or sting.
procedure: Examine each pest specimen with a hand lens and identify it.
State the crop it attacks, the part attacked, its mouthparts (biting/chewing or piercing/sucking) and the damage symptoms.
Walk a cowpea plot, pick 200 pods at random and count those with pod-borer holes.
Take 50 maize grains at random from a store and count those with weevil exit holes.
Calculate the percentage damage in each case.
Draw and label one pest and state one cultural, one chemical and one biological control method.

Stem borer larvae tunnel in maize stems (dead heart, broken stems). Weevils and bruchids leave small round exit holes and powdery frass in stored grain.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 34 of 200 cowpea pods were damaged: damage = 34 ÷ 200 × 100 = 17 %. 12 of 50 maize grains had weevil holes: 12 ÷ 50 × 100 = 24 %. If a store holds 500 kg of maize, the estimated damaged grain = 0.24 × 500 = 120 kg.
precautions: Sample at random across the whole plot or store, not just the obviously damaged parts.
Handle specimens gently to keep legs and antennae intact.
Label all specimen bottles.

Small or hidden holes missed.
Damage by one pest mistaken for another.

Recommending insecticide alone without cultural control.
Giving the damage percentage without showing the counts.

practicals.title: Crop diseases: symptoms, causal agents and disease incidence
practicals.topic: Practical: Main pests and diseases of crops
practicals.aim: To identify the main crop diseases from their symptoms, name the causal agents and estimate disease incidence on a plot.
materials: Diseased specimens or fresh samples: cassava mosaic, maize streak, rice blast, groundnut rosette, black pod of cocoa, leaf spot (Cercospora), damping-off seedlings, tomato wilt
safety: Wash hands after handling diseased material.
Bag diseased samples so spores are not spread to healthy plants.
Burn or bury removed diseased material.
procedure: Examine each specimen and describe the symptoms (mottling, streaks, spots, rot, wilting, stunting).
Name the disease, its causal organism type (virus, fungus, bacterium) and any vector.
On a cassava plot, examine 150 plants along fixed rows and count those with mosaic symptoms.
Calculate disease incidence.
Recommend prevention and control measures for each disease.
practicals.expectedObservations: Cassava mosaic: yellow-green mottled, distorted leaves, stunting (virus spread by whitefly). Maize streak: narrow yellow streaks along leaves (virus spread by leafhoppers). Black pod: brown-black rotting cocoa pods (fungus, Phytophthora). Damping-off: seedlings collapse at soil level (fungi). Groundnut rosette: stunted, bushy, yellowed plants (virus spread by aphids).
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 27 of 150 cassava plants showed mosaic. Disease incidence = 27 ÷ 150 × 100 = 18 %. If the whole field has 10 000 plants, the expected number infected = 0.18 × 10 000 = 1 800 plants.
precautions: Inspect plants systematically so none is counted twice.
Examine both leaf surfaces.
Use clean tools between plants.
sourcesOfError: Nutrient deficiency symptoms mistaken for disease.
Early infections without visible symptoms missed.
commonMistakes: Recommending fungicide for a viral disease.
Confusing the vector with the causal agent.
Not stating the organism type.
examTips: Answer format: disease – causal agent – symptoms – control.

Know the vectors: whitefly (cassava mosaic), leafhopper (maize streak), aphid (groundnut rosette).

practicals.title: Plant population, seed rate and planting dates
practicals.topic: Practical: Planting dates, seed rates, plant population and seed quality tests
practicals.aim: To calculate plant population and seed rate for a crop from its spacing, seed weight and germination percentage, and relate them to the planting date.
materials: Maize seed of known 1 000-seed weight and germination percentage
A 20 m × 15 m plot
safety: Wear gloves when handling seeds dressed with fungicide or insecticide.
Wash hands before eating.
procedure: Note the recommended planting date for the crop in your area (e.g. maize in southern Nigeria at the onset of rains, March–April for the early season).
Note the recommended spacing (e.g. maize 75 cm × 25 cm, one seed per hole).
Calculate the plant population per hectare and per plot.
Weigh 1 000 seeds (or 100 seeds × 10) to obtain the 1 000-seed weight.
Calculate the seed rate, adjusting for germination percentage.
Mark out the plot with lines and pegs at the chosen spacing and sow the plot.
practicals.expectedObservations: Plots sown at the correct spacing have uniform stands; seeds of low germination percentage need a higher seed rate to give the same stand.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: spacing 0.75 m × 0.25 m. Area per plant = 0.1875 m². Plant population = 10 000 ÷ 0.1875 = 53 333 plants/ha. 1 000-seed weight = 300 g. Seed needed = 53 333 × 0.300 g = 16 000 g = 16.0 kg/ha at 100 % germination. With 90 % germination, seed rate = 16.0 ÷ 0.90 = 17.8 kg/ha. For a 20 m × 15 m plot (300 m²): stands = 300 ÷ 0.1875 = 1 600.
precautions: Use a taut garden line so rows are straight and evenly spaced.
Weigh a fresh, representative sample of seeds.
Use the germination percentage of the actual seed lot.
sourcesOfError: Uneven spacing in the field.
Seed weight varies between lots.
Losses to pests and birds after sowing.
commonMistakes: Using cm instead of m in the population formula.
Multiplying by germination percentage instead of dividing.
Forgetting to account for seeds per hole.
examTips: Formula: plant population = area ÷ (inter-row × intra-row spacing) × seeds per stand.
Convert all spacings to metres before dividing into 10 000 m².
Planting dates: explain that sowing at the start of reliable rains reduces drought stress and some pest and disease attacks.

practicals.title: Seed quality tests: germination percentage and purity
practicals.topic: Practical: Planting dates, seed rates, plant population and seed quality tests
practicals.aim: To determine the germination percentage and purity of a seed lot and calculate the pure live seed percentage.
materials: A seed lot of maize, cowpea or rice (from the market or school store)
Water
Sand (optional, for a sand-tray test)
safety: Wear gloves when handling treated seed.
Keep the trays where they will not be knocked over.
procedure: Weigh a 50 g working sample and separate it into pure seed, weed seeds, other crop seeds and inert matter (stones, chaff); weigh the pure seed.
Calculate the purity percentage.
Count 100 pure seeds at random (or 4 lots of 25) and place them evenly on moist filter paper or cotton wool in Petri dishes.
Keep the dishes moist at room temperature and cover them to reduce drying.
After 5–7 days count the normal seedlings (with healthy radicle and plumule).
Calculate the germination percentage and the pure live seed (PLS) percentage, then adjust the seed rate.
practicals.expectedObservations: Most viable seeds swell and show a radicle within 2–4 days; dead or damaged seeds become soft, mouldy or remain hard and unchanged.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: of a 50.0 g sample, pure seed weighed 47.5 g (inert matter and weed seeds 2.5 g). Purity = 47.5 ÷ 50.0 × 100 = 95 %. Of 100 seeds, 84 germinated normally: germination = 84 %. Pure live seed = 0.95 × 0.84 × 100 = 79.8 %. If 16 kg/ha of perfect seed is needed, the actual seed rate = 16 ÷ 0.798 = 20.1 kg/ha.
precautions: Keep the filter paper moist but not flooded.
Choose seeds at random, not the biggest ones.
Count only normal seedlings as germinated.
sourcesOfError: Fungal growth spreads from dead to healthy seeds.
Uneven moisture or temperature.
Too few seeds in the sample.
commonMistakes: Counting swollen seeds without a radicle as germinated.
Using percentage purity alone to adjust the seed rate.
Leaving the dishes uncovered so they dry out.
examTips: Show the set-up: Petri dish, moist cotton wool or filter paper, evenly spaced seeds.
State the conditions for germination tested: water, oxygen, suitable temperature.
Give two reasons for a seed quality test: to decide seed rate and to avoid poor stands.

practicals.title: Seedbed preparation, transplanting and routine crop husbandry
practicals.topic: Practical: Seedbed preparation and crop husbandry operations
practicals.aim: To prepare a raised seedbed, transplant vegetable seedlings and carry out fertiliser application, mulching, watering and pest control.
apparatus: Cutlass, hoe, spade, rake, garden fork
materials: Tomato or pepper seedlings from the nursery (4–6 weeks old)
Dry grass for mulch
Well-rotted poultry manure
A recommended insecticide
safety: Wear gloves, mask and boots when spraying; spray with the wind behind you.
Keep pesticides locked away and never transfer them into drink bottles.
Do not eat or drink while handling chemicals; wash afterwards.
procedure: Clear the site, remove stumps and debris and dig the soil to about 20 cm deep.
Mark out a bed 10 m long and 1.2 m wide with pegs and line; raise it about 15–20 cm, breaking clods and working in manure.
Level the bed with a rake and mark two rows 60 cm apart with plants 50 cm apart in each row.
Water the nursery and the bed; lift seedlings with a ball of soil and transplant them in the evening at the marked points.
Water immediately and mulch between the rows with dry grass.
Two weeks after transplanting, apply NPK in a ring about 5–10 cm from each plant and cover with soil.
Weed regularly, stake tomato plants and spray against pests when needed, following the label.
practicals.expectedObservations: Well-raised, fine-tilth beds drain well and seedlings establish quickly. Seedlings transplanted with a ball of soil in the evening suffer less wilting. Mulched areas stay moist longer and have fewer weeds.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: bed 10 m long with plants every 0.5 m including both ends gives 10 ÷ 0.5 + 1 = 21 plants per row; with 2 rows = 42 plants. At 5 g of NPK per plant, fertiliser needed = 42 × 5 = 210 g. With 5 such beds, total = 5 × 210 = 1 050 g = 1.05 kg.
precautions: Transplant in the cool of the evening or on a cloudy day.
Do not let fertiliser touch the stem.
Harden off seedlings before transplanting.
sourcesOfError: Uneven spacing.
Rough estimate of fertiliser using cups instead of weighing.
commonMistakes: Planting seedlings deeper or shallower than in the nursery.
Applying fertiliser on dry soil without watering.
Spraying against the wind.
examTips: Number the steps of seedbed preparation in the correct order: clearing, tilling, bed making, levelling.
Give reasons for operations: mulching conserves moisture, suppresses weeds, adds organic matter.
Calculation questions often combine row count and fertiliser per plant.

practicals.title: Identifying forest products and by-products; log volume
practicals.topic: Practical: Forest products and by-products
practicals.aim: To identify common forest products and by-products and calculate the volume and value of a log.
materials: Specimens: sawn timber, plywood, particle board, charcoal, firewood, rattan cane, chewing stick, kola nuts, honey, shea butter, gum arabic, raffia, bamboo, bush mango (ogbono) seeds, medicinal bark, a short log section
safety: Beware of splinters; wear gloves.
Keep charcoal and firewood specimens away from flames.
procedure: Identify each specimen and classify it as a timber product, non-timber forest product (NTFP) or by-product (e.g. sawdust).
State one use of each and the tree or plant it comes from.
Measure the length of the log section and its mid-length diameter.
Calculate the log volume with Huber's formula, V = π(d/2)²L.
Calculate the value of the log at a given price per cubic metre.

practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a log is 6.0 m long with a mid-diameter of 0.50 m. Radius = 0.25 m. Volume = 3.142 × 0.25² × 6.0 = 1.178 m³. At ₦60 000 per m³ the log is worth 1.178 × ₦60 000 = ₦70 680.

Record units in metres before calculating.
Handle specimens gently to keep them for future classes.

Bark thickness included in the diameter.

Mixing centimetres and metres.
Listing plywood as a non-timber product.
examTips: Specimen questions: identify, state the source plant and one use.
Know the difference between products (timber, NTFPs) and by-products (sawdust, wood shavings, bark).
Give the formula with units in log-volume questions.

practicals.title: Propagation of horticultural plants: layering, budding and grafting
practicals.topic: Practical: Methods of propagation of horticultural plants
practicals.aim: To carry out direct sowing, transplanting, layering, budding and grafting and calculate the success rate.
materials: Citrus rootstock seedlings (e.g. rough lemon) and budwood from a high-yielding sweet orange
Mango rootstocks and scions
Ixora or Bougainvillea for layering
Seeds for direct sowing
safety: Cut away from the body on a firm support.
Close and sheath knives when not in use.
Treat cuts on hands immediately.
procedure: Direct sowing: sow seeds in polybags or beds at the correct depth and water.
Simple layering: bend a low branch of Ixora, wound the underside, peg it into the soil, cover with soil and keep moist; sever after roots form.
Air layering (marcotting): ring the bark of a branch, wrap moist rooting medium in polythene around the wound, tie both ends.
T-budding: make a T-shaped cut on the rootstock 20–25 cm above the soil, lift the bark flaps, slide in a shield bud from the budwood and tie firmly with budding tape, leaving the bud exposed.
Cleft grafting: cut the rootstock across, split it, insert a wedge-shaped scion with matching cambium and tie.
After 2–3 weeks remove ties and check whether buds and scions remain green (successful 'take'); cut back the rootstock above successful buds.
Record numbers and calculate the percentage success.
practicals.expectedObservations: Successful buds stay green and plump and later sprout; failed buds turn brown and shrivel. Layered branches form roots at the wound in 4–8 weeks.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 40 citrus seedlings were budded and 32 buds took. Success = 32 ÷ 40 × 100 = 80 %. Materials cost ₦8 000, so the cost per successful budded plant = ₦8 000 ÷ 32 = ₦250.
precautions: Use clean, sharp knives so cuts are smooth.
Match the cambium layers of stock and scion.
Tie firmly to exclude air and water, and shade newly grafted plants.
sourcesOfError: Differences in skill between students.
Budwood allowed to dry out.
commonMistakes: Covering the bud with tape so it cannot sprout.
Using a diseased or low-yielding budwood source.
Leaving the tie on too long so it strangles the stem.
examTips: Know the terms: stock (rootstock), scion, budwood, cambium, union.
State advantages: early fruiting, true-to-type plants, combining good root and shoot qualities.
Drawings of a T-bud and cleft graft are commonly requested; label stock, scion/bud and tie.

checkQuestions.explanation: The scion forms the shoot; the rootstock provides roots.

practicals.title: Identifying common weeds and estimating weed density
practicals.topic: Practical: Common weeds
practicals.aim: To identify common weeds by their external features, state their modes of dispersal and control, and estimate weed density with a quadrat.
materials: Weedy plot on the school farm

Specimens: spear grass (Imperata cylindrica), goat weed (Ageratum conyzoides), Siam weed (Chromolaena odorata), Tridax procumbens, sedge (Cyperus rotundus), Euphorbia heterophylla, Striga, water hyacinth (picture)
safety: Wear gloves; some weeds have sharp edges or irritant sap.
Watch out for snakes and stinging insects in tall weeds.
procedure: Examine each weed specimen: leaf shape and venation, stem, root type, flower or seed, any underground organs (rhizome, tuber).
State whether it is a grass, sedge or broadleaf weed and annual or perennial.
State its mode of dispersal (wind, animals, water, rhizomes).
Throw the quadrat at random five times in the weedy plot and count all weeds inside, recording each species.
Calculate the mean weed density and the frequency of each species.
Recommend cultural, mechanical, chemical and biological control methods.
practicals.expectedObservations: Spear grass: narrow leaves with sharp tips and an extensive white rhizome system – perennial, hard to control. Tridax: hairy broadleaf with yellow flower heads and plumed fruits spread by wind. Cyperus: triangular stem, tubers (nuts). Chromolaena: aromatic shrub with tiny wind-dispersed fruits.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: weed counts in five 1 m² quadrats were 12, 8, 15, 10 and 5. Total = 50, so mean density = 50 ÷ 5 = 10 weeds/m². Tridax was present in 4 of the 5 quadrats, giving a frequency of 4 ÷ 5 × 100 = 80 %. For a 0.1 ha (1 000 m²) plot, the estimated weed population = 10 × 1 000 = 10 000 weeds.
precautions: Throw the quadrat at random without aiming.
Count weeds rooted inside the quadrat only; decide a rule for plants on the edge.
Use the same quadrat size throughout.
sourcesOfError: Too few quadrats for a patchy weed distribution.
Seedlings missed or misidentified.
commonMistakes: Using botanical names without the common name (or vice versa) when both are asked.
Recommending hand-pulling for spear grass (rhizomes regrow).
Dividing the total by the number of species instead of the number of quadrats.
examTips: Give an identifying feature with each name.
Link dispersal method to a structure: plumed fruit – wind; hooks – animals.
List harmful effects: competition, harbouring pests, reducing quality, parasitism (Striga).

practicals.title: Identifying breeds of farm animals; restraint, handling and growth records
practicals.topic: Practical: Common breeds and types of animals
practicals.aim: To identify common local and exotic breeds of farm animals, restrain and handle them safely, and calculate daily weight gain.
apparatus: Weighing scale (spring balance or platform scale)
materials: Animals on the school farm or a nearby farm: e.g. White Fulani and N'Dama cattle, West African Dwarf and Red Sokoto goats, Yankasa and Balami sheep, Large White pig, Isa Brown layers, broilers, local chickens (or clear pictures)
safety: Approach animals calmly from the side, never directly from behind.
Keep clear of horns, hooves and kicking legs; work with the farm attendant.
Wash hands after handling animals (zoonoses).
procedure: Observe each animal and record its colour, size, horn shape, ears, hump, hair or wool, and its main use (meat, milk, eggs, draught).
Name the breed and state whether it is local (indigenous) or exotic.
Restrain a goat by holding it under the jaw and around the rump against your legs; halter cattle; hold poultry with wings folded against the body and legs held.
Groom the animal with a brush and examine the skin, eyes and feet for health signs.
Weigh the animal (or estimate weight with a weigh band) and record it.
Use two weight records to calculate the average daily gain.
practicals.expectedObservations: White Fulani: white with black ears and muzzle, large lyre-shaped horns and a hump – dual purpose. N'Dama: humpless, fawn-coloured, trypanotolerant. West African Dwarf goat: small, short-legged, hardy. Red Sokoto: reddish-brown, prized skin. Large White pig: white, erect ears, long body.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a West African Dwarf goat weighed 18.0 kg on 1 March and 24.6 kg 60 days later. Weight gain = 24.6 − 18.0 = 6.6 kg. Average daily gain = 6.6 ÷ 60 = 0.110 kg = 110 g per day.
precautions: Weigh animals at the same time of day, before feeding.
Use gentle, firm restraint to avoid injuring the animal.
Check that the scale reads zero before weighing.
sourcesOfError: Gut fill varies with feeding and drinking.
Weigh-band estimates are approximate.
Animal moving on the scale.
commonMistakes: Confusing N'Dama (humpless) with White Fulani (humped).
Dividing weight gain by weeks when the question asks per day.
Handling poultry by the wings or neck.
examTips: Identification questions: breed, one distinguishing feature, one use.
Know local versus exotic advantages: hardiness and disease tolerance versus higher productivity.
Give daily gain in g/day or kg/day with units.

practicals.title: Major internal organs of farm animals (dissection and dressing percentage)
practicals.topic: Practical: Major internal organs of farm animals
practicals.aim: To identify the digestive, reproductive and excretory organs of a ruminant and a bird, state their functions and calculate dressing percentage.
materials: A freshly slaughtered chicken from the school farm or market
Ruminant viscera from an abattoir (or a goat being processed), or charts
safety: Wear gloves and an apron; cover cuts.
Use sharp instruments carefully and cut away from yourself.
Dispose of offal hygienically and disinfect the tray and benches.
procedure: Weigh the live bird or animal before slaughter (or record the given live weight).
After slaughter and bleeding, open the body cavity along the mid-ventral line.

Identify the organs of the digestive system: in the bird – oesophagus, crop, proventriculus, gizzard, small intestine, caeca, cloaca; in the ruminant – rumen, reticulum, omasum, abomasum, small and large intestines.
Identify the liver, heart, lungs, kidneys and reproductive organs (ovary and oviduct in the hen; testes in males).
Draw and label the digestive system of the fowl and state the function of each part.
Weigh the dressed carcass (without head, feet, skin or feathers and viscera) and calculate the dressing percentage.
practicals.expectedObservations: The fowl has a crop for storage, a glandular proventriculus and a muscular gizzard containing grit for grinding. The ruminant stomach has four compartments; the rumen is the largest and is full of fermenting feed. Kidneys are paired and bean-shaped in mammals, lobed in birds.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a goat with a live weight of 30.0 kg gave a carcass of 14.4 kg. Dressing percentage = carcass weight ÷ live weight × 100 = 14.4 ÷ 30.0 × 100 = 48 %. A broiler of 2.0 kg live weight dressed at 72 % gives a carcass of 2.0 × 0.72 = 1.44 kg.
precautions: Make shallow cuts so the gut is not pierced.
Spread out the organs in their natural positions before drawing.
Weigh carcasses on a calibrated scale.
sourcesOfError: Differences in what is removed in dressing.
Gut fill affecting live weight.
commonMistakes: Calling the gizzard the 'stomach' without noting it is muscular and grinds food.
Drawing the ruminant stomach with three compartments.
Dividing live weight by carcass weight.
examTips: Function marks: crop – stores and softens food; gizzard – grinds food; rumen – microbial fermentation of cellulose.

practicals.title: Identifying animal by-products and their uses
practicals.topic: Practical: Animal by-products
practicals.aim: To identify animal by-products and state their uses, and estimate the quantity of a by-product from a batch of animals.
materials: Specimens: hides and skins, feathers, horns, hooves, bones (bone meal), blood meal, wool or hair, poultry droppings, cow dung, snail shells
safety: Wear gloves; raw by-products can carry anthrax and other pathogens.
Wash hands thoroughly after the practical.
Keep specimens dry and covered to avoid flies.
procedure: Examine each specimen and name it.
State the animal it comes from.
State at least one use (e.g. hides – leather; feathers – feather meal, pillows; horns and hooves – buttons, glue; bones – bone meal; blood – blood meal; dung – manure, biogas).
State how each is processed or preserved (e.g. salting and drying hides).
Calculate the expected quantity of a by-product from a batch of animals.

practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: feathers make up about 7 % of the live weight of a broiler. A batch of 500 broilers each weighing 2.0 kg gives feathers of 500 × 2.0 × 0.07 = 70 kg. If processed feather meal sells at ₦400 per kg and processing yields 80 % of the raw mass, income = 70 × 0.80 × ₦400 = ₦22 400.
precautions: Handle raw by-products with gloves.
Label every specimen clearly.
Store dried specimens in airtight containers.

Confusing hides (large animals) with skins (small animals).
Giving 'fertiliser' as the only use for every by-product.
examTips: Give the by-product, its source animal and one use – three marks per specimen.
Mention that blood meal and bone meal are feed ingredients (protein, calcium and phosphorus).
Hides are preserved by salting, sun-drying or wet-salting before tanning.

practicals.title: Identifying feedstuffs and formulating a ration by Pearson square
practicals.topic: Practical: Animal feeds and feed stuffs
practicals.aim: To identify common feedstuffs and their main nutrients and use the Pearson square to formulate a ration of a given crude protein level.
materials: Samples: maize, sorghum, wheat offal, rice bran, groundnut cake, soya bean meal, palm kernel cake, fish meal, blood meal, bone meal, oyster shell, salt, vitamin–mineral premix, cassava peel
safety: Wear a dust mask when handling dusty feeds.
Do not taste feeds; fish meal and blood meal may carry Salmonella.
Keep feeds away from rodents and moisture (aflatoxin).
procedure: Examine each feedstuff and record colour, texture and smell.
Classify each as an energy feed, protein concentrate (plant or animal), mineral supplement, vitamin supplement or roughage.
State the local source of each (e.g. groundnut cake from groundnut oil mills).
Choose an energy source and a protein source and note their crude protein (CP) contents.
Draw a Pearson square with the target CP in the centre and calculate the parts and percentages of each ingredient.
Calculate the mass of each ingredient for the batch size required and check the CP of the mixture.
practicals.expectedObservations: Maize: yellow grains, high energy, about 9 % CP. Soya bean meal and groundnut cake: brown flakes or powder, 40–45 % CP. Fish meal: brown, strong fishy smell, about 60–65 % CP. Oyster shell: white fragments (calcium). Wheat offal and rice bran: fibrous brown powder.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: make 100 kg of an 18 % CP ration from maize (9 % CP) and soya bean meal (44 % CP). Pearson square: maize parts = 44 − 18 = 26; soya parts = 18 − 9 = 9; total parts = 35. Maize = 26 ÷ 35 × 100 = 74.29 %; soya = 9 ÷ 35 × 100 = 25.71 %. For 100 kg: 74.3 kg maize and 25.7 kg soya bean meal. Check: 0.7429 × 9 + 0.2571 × 44 = 6.69 + 11.31 = 18.0 % CP.
precautions: The target CP must lie between the CP values of the two ingredients.
Subtract diagonally and ignore negative signs.
Mix ingredients thoroughly so every portion has the same composition.
sourcesOfError: Actual CP of local feedstuffs differs from book values.
Weighing errors when mixing.
commonMistakes: Placing the parts against the wrong ingredient (parts go across the diagonal to the opposite corner).
Choosing a target CP outside the range of the two feeds.
Forgetting to check the answer.
examTips: Draw the square neatly with labels; examiners award marks for the diagram.
Classify feeds correctly: maize – energy; fish meal – animal protein; oyster shell – mineral.
State factors in ration formulation: age and class of animal, nutrient needs, cost, availability, palatability.

practicals.title: Ectoparasites and endoparasites of farm animals and deworming doses
practicals.topic: Practical: Main pests and parasites of farm animals
practicals.aim: To identify common ecto- and endoparasites of farm animals, describe their damage and life cycles, and calculate drug doses for control.
materials: Preserved specimens or charts: ticks, lice, mites, fleas, tsetse fly, tapeworm segments, liver fluke, roundworm (Ascaris)
A dewormer bottle label (for dose reading)
safety: Handle parasites with forceps; wear gloves.
Preserved specimens are often in formalin – avoid inhaling or skin contact.
Wash hands thoroughly; several parasites infect humans.
procedure: Examine each specimen with a hand lens and record size, segmentation, number of legs, mouthparts and body shape.
Classify each as an ectoparasite or endoparasite and name its host(s).
State the damage caused and the disease it may transmit.
Outline the life cycle of the tick or the tapeworm (eggs, intermediate host, adult).
Draw and label one parasite.
Read the dose rate from the dewormer label and calculate doses for animals of given weights.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ticks: eight legs, unsegmented oval body, swell when engorged with blood. Lice: small, flattened, six legs, cling to hair. Tapeworm: long, flat, ribbon-like, segmented (proglottids). Liver fluke: flat, leaf-shaped, found in bile ducts. Roundworm: cylindrical, unsegmented, pointed at both ends.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: a dewormer label states 1 mL per 10 kg body weight. A 35 kg goat needs 35 ÷ 10 × 1 = 3.5 mL. A flock of 20 goats averaging 25 kg needs 20 × 2.5 mL = 50 mL in total, so one 100 mL bottle is enough with 50 mL left.
precautions: Weigh animals (or estimate weight accurately) before dosing to avoid under- or over-dosing.
Follow the label withdrawal period before slaughter or selling milk.
Store specimens in labelled bottles.
sourcesOfError: Estimated body weights lead to wrong doses.
Damaged specimens are hard to identify.
commonMistakes: Calling a tick an insect (it is an arachnid with eight legs).
Confusing the intermediate host of the liver fluke (water snail) with the final host.
Using the same dose for all animals regardless of weight.
examTips: Answer pattern: name – host – damage – control.
Know intermediate hosts: liver fluke – snail; beef tapeworm – cattle (human final host).
Control of ectoparasites: dipping, spraying, hand-picking; endoparasites: deworming (drenching), rotational grazing, hygiene.
