practicals.title: Preventing and controlling livestock diseases: dipping, spraying, drenching and sanitation
practicals.topic: Practical: Diseases of farm animals
practicals.aim: To carry out (or demonstrate) disease prevention and control practices and correctly dilute an acaricide for spraying.
materials: Acaricide concentrate (label read for dilution)
Disinfectant
Water
Animals on the school or nearby farm
safety: Wear protective clothing and do not eat, drink or smoke while handling chemicals.
Spray downwind of yourself and keep chemicals away from water sources and children.
Dispose of empty containers safely (puncture and bury); never reuse them.
procedure: Observe animals for signs of ill-health: dullness, loss of appetite, discharges, diarrhoea, coughing, rough coat, abnormal temperature.
Take the rectal temperature of a goat and compare it with the normal range (about 38.5–40 °C).
Read the acaricide label and measure the correct volume of concentrate for the volume of water in the sprayer.
Spray the animals thoroughly, especially the ears, under the tail, between the legs and the udder or scrotum.
Demonstrate drenching: hold the head level, insert the drenching gun at the corner of the mouth over the tongue and deliver slowly.
Clean and disinfect pens, feeders and drinkers; refill the footbath with disinfectant at the pen entrance.
Record treatments and dates in the health record.
practicals.expectedObservations: Healthy animals are alert with bright eyes and a smooth coat; sick animals isolate themselves, have dull eyes and may have a raised temperature. Ticks die and drop off within days of correct acaricide treatment.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: the label states 2 mL of concentrate per litre of water. A 15-litre knapsack sprayer needs 2 × 15 = 30 mL. To spray a herd requiring 4 full tanks, total concentrate = 4 × 30 = 120 mL.
precautions: Use the exact label dilution; too strong is toxic, too weak causes resistance.
Do not drench too fast or with the head raised high, or liquid may enter the lungs.
Isolate sick animals and new arrivals (quarantine).
sourcesOfError: Inaccurate measurement of the concentrate.
Incomplete coverage of the animal's body.
commonMistakes: Mixing the concentrate without measuring.
Raising the animal's head high during drenching.
Confusing prevention (vaccination, sanitation) with treatment (drugs).
examTips: Describe each control method with a purpose: dipping/spraying – ectoparasites; drenching – endoparasites; vaccination – viral and bacterial diseases.
List farm sanitation practices: cleaning pens, footbaths, proper disposal of dead animals, quarantine.
Dilution questions: concentrate = rate × volume of water.

practicals.title: Routine management practices: identification, debeaking, castration and culling
practicals.topic: Practical: Routine management practices in farm animals
practicals.aim: To identify tools for routine management practices, describe how the practices are done, and read and assign ear-notch numbers.
apparatus: Ear-notcher, ear tags and applicator, tattoo pliers and ink, branding iron
materials: Piglets, kids or chicks on the school farm (demonstration by the farm attendant or veterinarian), or pictures
Antiseptic spray or wound oil
safety: Only trained staff should perform castration, debeaking and dehorning; students observe.
Restrain animals properly to avoid injury to animal and handler.
Apply antiseptic to wounds and keep pens clean to prevent infection.
procedure: Identify each tool and state the practice it is used for.
Observe ear-notching of piglets and note where notches are placed according to the farm's numbering system.
Observe debeaking of pullets (removing the tip of the upper beak) to prevent cannibalism and feather pecking.
Observe bloodless castration of a buck or bull calf using the burdizzo, or castration with an elastrator ring in young lambs.
Examine the flock or herd records and select animals for breeding or culling (poor layers, sick, old, infertile animals).
Record each practice, the date and the animal identity.
practicals.expectedObservations: Ear notches remain as permanent marks that identify each pig. Debeaked birds peck less at each other. Castrated males become calmer and fatten better. Poor layers have a pale, small, dry comb, yellow-pigmented shanks and narrow pubic bones.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example (using the system on this farm): right ear – notch on lower edge = 1, upper edge = 3; left ear – lower edge = 10, upper edge = 30. Pig number 47 = 30 + 10 (left ear, one upper and one lower notch) + 3 + 3 + 1 (right ear, two upper and one lower notch) = 40 + 7 = 47. Culling: a flock of 500 layers produced 300 eggs a day. Hen-day production = 300 ÷ 500 × 100 = 60 %; after culling 50 poor layers egg output fell only to 295, giving 295 ÷ 450 × 100 = 65.6 %.
precautions: Use clean, disinfected tools.
Perform practices at the recommended age (e.g. castration and notching of piglets in the first weeks).
Keep accurate identity records.
sourcesOfError: Different farms use different ear-notch systems; always use the stated key.
Misreading notches on dirty or torn ears.
commonMistakes: Confusing the burdizzo (castration) with the debeaker.
Adding notch values from the wrong ear.
Culling only on age rather than performance.
examTips: For each practice give: tool, animal, reason and age.
Ear-notch questions always provide the key – read it carefully before adding.
List methods of identification: ear-notching, tagging, tattooing, branding, leg bands (poultry).

practicals.title: Fish harvesting, processing and preservation (smoking)
practicals.topic: Practical: Fish harvesting and preservation
practicals.aim: To describe and carry out methods of harvesting and preserving fish, and calculate the weight loss and moisture content after smoking.
materials: Catfish (Clarias) or tilapia from the school pond or a local fish farm
Clean water, salt
Firewood or charcoal
safety: Take care near ponds; never work alone at the water's edge.
Catfish have sharp pectoral spines – hold firmly behind the head.
Keep a safe distance from the kiln fire and smoke; ensure good ventilation.
procedure: Lower the pond water level, drag the net from one end to the other and scoop out the fish.
Sort fish by size; keep those for sale chilled on ice.
Weigh the fish to be preserved (fresh weight).
Kill humanely, gut, wash and, if required, salt the fish lightly.
Arrange the fish on the wire racks of the smoking kiln and smoke-dry over a slow fire, turning them, for several hours until dry and golden brown.
Cool and weigh the smoked fish.
Calculate the percentage weight loss and the moisture content of the product; store in a cool, dry, airy place.
practicals.expectedObservations: Smoked fish become firm, dry, golden to dark brown, with a smoky smell, and lose much of their weight. Poorly smoked fish remain soft and quickly turn mouldy.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example: 20.0 kg of fresh catfish (75 % water) was smoked to 7.0 kg. Weight loss = 20.0 − 7.0 = 13.0 kg = 13.0 ÷ 20.0 × 100 = 65 %. Dry matter = 20.0 × 0.25 = 5.0 kg, which is unchanged, so water left = 7.0 − 5.0 = 2.0 kg and the moisture content of the smoked fish = 2.0 ÷ 7.0 × 100 = 28.6 %.
precautions: Process fish quickly after harvest to prevent spoilage.
Use a slow, even fire so fish dry rather than burn.
Store smoked fish off the floor in insect-proof containers.
sourcesOfError: Fish not uniformly dried.
Weighing smoked fish while still hot.
commonMistakes: Calling smoking 'cooking' – its purpose is to remove water.
Using a fierce fire that chars the outside and leaves the inside moist.
Confusing weight loss with moisture content of the product.
examTips: List preservation methods: chilling/icing, freezing, smoking, sun-drying, salting, canning, frying.
Explain the principle: removing water or lowering temperature slows bacteria and enzymes.
Name harvesting gear: drag (seine) net, cast net, scoop net, hook and line, traps.

checkQuestions.explanation: Dryness and smoke chemicals slow microbial growth.

checkQuestions.explanation: A seine net is pulled across the pond.

checkQuestions.explanation: Chilling slows spoilage.

practicals.title: Keeping farm records; depreciation and profit and loss account
practicals.topic: Farm records and accounts
practicals.aim: To design farm records and use them to calculate depreciation and prepare a simple profit and loss account for a broiler enterprise.
apparatus: Record books (inventory, production, sales and purchases)
materials: Data from the school poultry unit or the worked example below
safety: Keep records in a dry, secure place; back up important figures.
procedure: Design an inventory record listing each asset, date bought, cost, expected life and salvage value.
Design a production record (e.g. daily feed use, mortality, weights) and a sales and purchases record.
Calculate annual depreciation of equipment using the straight-line method.
Calculate the book value after a given number of years.
List all costs (variable and fixed) and all revenue for one batch.
Prepare a profit and loss account and state whether the enterprise made a profit.
practicals.expectedObservations: Complete records show where money is spent and earned, allow profit to be measured and support loan applications.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example 1: an incubator cost ₦500 000, has a salvage value of ₦50 000 and a life of 5 years. Annual depreciation = (500 000 − 50 000) ÷ 5 = ₦90 000. Book value after 2 years = 500 000 − 2 × 90 000 = ₦320 000. Worked example 2 (400 broilers): costs – day-old chicks 400 × ₦800 = ₦320 000; feed 400 × 4 kg × ₦600 = ₦960 000; drugs and vaccines ₦60 000; labour ₦120 000; depreciation share ₦30 000; total ₦1 490 000. With 5 % mortality, 380 birds sold at ₦5 500 = ₦2 090 000. Profit = 2 090 000 − 1 490 000 = ₦600 000.
precautions: Record transactions on the day they happen.
Keep receipts for all purchases.
Separate fixed costs from variable costs.
sourcesOfError: Unrecorded small expenses.
Estimated useful life and salvage values.
commonMistakes: Forgetting to subtract the salvage value in straight-line depreciation.
Counting all birds as sold despite mortality.
Treating the full price of equipment as a cost of one batch.
examTips: Show the formula: depreciation = (cost − salvage value) ÷ useful life.
Lay out profit and loss in two columns (expenditure and income) with totals.
Know the record types: inventory, production, income and expenditure, and special records (e.g. breeding, health).

checkQuestions.explanation: An inventory lists what the farm owns.

practicals.title: Crop improvement: monohybrid and dihybrid ratios with seeds
practicals.topic: Crop improvement
practicals.aim: To demonstrate Mendel's laws by counting seed phenotypes in segregating maize cobs (or model beads) and comparing them with expected ratios.
materials: F2 maize cobs segregating for purple and yellow kernels (and smooth/wrinkled where available), or two colours of beads/beans in bags as a model
safety: Do not eat treated or coloured seeds.
Wash hands after handling seeds.
procedure: Explain the cross: a pure purple (PP) parent crossed with pure yellow (pp) gives F1 all purple (Pp); F1 self-pollinated gives the F2 cob.
Count purple and yellow kernels on an F2 cob (or draw pairs of beads at random from two bags each containing equal numbers of P and p beads).
Record the totals and calculate the observed ratio.
Compare with the expected 3 : 1 ratio.
For a dihybrid cob (colour and texture), count the four classes and compare with 9 : 3 : 3 : 1.
Relate the results to selection and breeding in crop improvement.
practicals.expectedObservations: About three-quarters of the kernels are purple and one-quarter yellow, close to 3 : 1. Dihybrid cobs show four kernel types in roughly 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 proportion.
practicals.dataAndCalculations: Worked example 1: an F2 cob had 312 purple and 104 yellow kernels. Total = 416; ratio = 312 ÷ 104 = 3.0 : 1. Expected purple = 3/4 × 416 = 312, yellow = 104 – an exact fit. Worked example 2: a cross of tall (TT) × dwarf (tt) gives F1 Tt; among 400 F2 plants expect 3/4 × 400 = 300 tall and 100 dwarf. Worked example 3: among 320 dihybrid F2 seeds expect 9/16 × 320 = 180, 3/16 × 320 = 60, 60 and 1/16 × 320 = 20.
precautions: Count each kernel once only; mark the starting row.
Draw beads without looking and replace them each time.
Use large numbers so the ratio approaches the expected value.
sourcesOfError: Kernels damaged or of intermediate colour.
Small samples deviate from expected ratios by chance.
commonMistakes: Expecting exact ratios in small samples.
Confusing genotype ratio (1 : 2 : 1) with phenotype ratio (3 : 1).
Writing the dominant allele in lower case.
examTips: Show the cross with a Punnett square, gametes and the F2 ratio.
State Mendel's first law (segregation) and second law (independent assortment) in words.
Link to crop improvement: selection, hybridisation, introduction and their aims (yield, disease resistance, quality).

checkQuestions.explanation: Three dominant phenotypes to one recessive.

checkQuestions.q: Among 240 F2 plants from Tt × Tt, the expected number of dwarf plants is
A cross of Tt × tt gives offspring in the ratio
checkQuestions.explanation: Half Tt (tall), half tt (dwarf).

checkQuestions.q: Mendel's second law describes
checkQuestions.explanation: Genes for different characters assort independently into gametes.
